extracted.intended_audience: school students (grades 8–11), teachers, local organizing committees and town organizers
extracted.subtask_description: Official descriptive rules and evaluation standards for the Tournament of Towns mathematical competition: eligibility, rounds/levels structure, scoring and result determination, awards, and organizational/participation guidance for students and local committees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and pedagogical aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament of Towns is an international mathematical Olympiad devoted not to sport success but to deep consideration of problems; it helps to develop qualities necessary for scientific research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes depth of thought and development of research-like qualities over mere contest ranking; organizers and problems should prioritize problems that encourage deep consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility by grade
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament is for school students of grades 8–11 (if 11 is the last grade). Any school student of any grade can participate in the Tournament for his grade or higher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students may enter at their own grade level or choose to participate at a higher grade level; explicit target grades are 8–11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounds and schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament has two rounds each year: Fall and Spring. (Example dates listed for 2025/2026: Fall — Oct 5 O-level / Oct 19 A-level; Spring — Mar 1 O-level / Mar 15 A-level.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounds are held annually in the fall and spring; local committees should follow the scheduled dates for their year. Participation in both rounds is optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels and comparative difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Each round has two levels — O-level (basic) and A-level (advanced). The A-level is comparable in difficulty with the All-Russian and International Mathematical Olympiads; the O-level is somewhat simpler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose level (O or A) appropriate to competitors' skills; A-level problems are intended to match high national/international olympiad difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junior and Senior subdivisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Each level is held separately for Juniors (grades 8–9) and Seniors (grades 10–11).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitors are grouped by Junior/Senior within each level; local organizers must administer separate exams or classifications for these age groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation optionality
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not obligatory to participate in all rounds or levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students may choose which rounds and levels to enter; missing a round does not preclude future participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring: three best problems counted
rubrics_metrics.description: For each participant, three best marks for problems are taken into account on each level of each round. The score of a participant is the sum of points for these three problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing a participant's result for a given level-round, select the three problems on which the participant scored highest (if problems have parts, use the summed marks per problem) and sum their points to produce the participant's level-round score.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-part aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a problem has separate parts then the marks for them are summed up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat multi-part problems as a single problem by summing subpart marks before selecting the three best problem scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final result determination across rounds/levels
rubrics_metrics.description: The final result is detected as the maximum on the results of each level of each round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A participant's overall/final result is the maximum of their level-round scores across the rounds and levels they entered (i.e., the best single result achieved).

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards and advancement criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants who showed sufficiently high results are awarded with Tournament diplomas. Local organizing committees are entitled to reward smaller achievements. Students with outstanding results receive an invitation to the annual Summer Conference of the Tournament of Towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awarding thresholds are determined so that 'sufficiently high' results merit diplomas; local committees may set additional or lesser recognitions. Exceptional performers are selected for Summer Conference invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost and local contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in the Tournament is free for all school students. Local organizing committees make voluntary money contributions if possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No mandatory participation fee; local committees may solicit voluntary contributions to cover local costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and expandability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tournament is organized by local committees in more than 100 cities across more than 25 countries; any town can participate in the contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local committees are responsible for local administration; the Tournament is designed to be widely adoptable — any town may form a local committee and join the contest network.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summer Conference selection & cultural tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Outstanding students are invited to the annual Summer Conference of the Tournament of Towns. An indispensable participant of these meetings is the samovar, which became the symbol of the International mathematical Tournament of Towns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection for the Summer Conference is by outstanding results; the Conference has established traditions (e.g., samovar symbol) important to its culture and identity.
